"title": "Coherent network analysis for triggered gravitational wave burst searches",
"authors": "K Hayama, S D Mohanty, M Rakhmanov, S Desai",
"field_subfield": "Gravitational-wave data analysis (triggered burst searches)",
"type_of_paper": "Methodology with simulated-data validation",
"executive_summary": "This paper introduces RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline for triggered gravitational-wave (GW) burst searches, and validates it with Monte Carlo simulations on a LIGO–Virgo network. The authors argue that triggered searches differ fundamentally from all-sky, untriggered searches in two ways. First, astronomical triggers such as gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) provide rich prior information—sky location, distance, and signal morphology—which should be exploited in the analysis. Second, the small data volume of triggered searches permits the use of computationally expensive algorithms, including advanced data conditioning, that are impractical in high-volume untriggered searches. Statistically, the reduction in parameter-space search volume yields higher sensitivity than untriggered searches. RIDGE implements two novel components: a two-step data conditioning procedure (running-median noise-floor estimation, FIR whitening, and MBLT line removal) and a regularized maximum-likelihood coherent network detection statistic. The detection statistic is evaluated via two forms, Rmm (max/min of the sky-map) and Rrad (radial distance in a scaled statistic plane), with Rrad shown to outperform Rmm. Simulations used the design sensitivity curves of the 4 km LIGO detectors (H1, L1), the 2 km LIGO detector (H2), and Virgo (V1), with Gaussian stationary noise and injected sinusoidal artifacts. Signals were sine-Gaussian with center frequency 235 Hz and Q = 9, located at the real GRB060813 trigger (θ = −30°, φ = 167.0°), with hrss values of 3 × 10⁻²², 5 × 10⁻²², and 7 × 10⁻²² Hz⁻¹ᐟ². ROC curves demonstrate that Rrad outperforms Rmm, and an hrss of 5 × 10⁻²² Hz⁻¹ᐟ² is detectable with ≈62% probability at a false-alarm probability of 10⁻². The authors conclude that RIDGE is sensitive, algorithmically distinct from existing pipelines, and suitable as an independent check and platform for new regulators. The paper is notable for its transparency about simulation choices and limitations, including the use of long integration times that yield lower-bound performance estimates and the absence of reported computational resources, ablation studies, or real-data validation. The bibliography is omitted, so top_influential_citations is empty.",

summary.title: Coherent network analysis for triggered gravitational wave burst searches
summary.authors: K Hayama, S D Mohanty, M Rakhmanov, S Desai
summary.field_subfield: Gravitational-wave data analysis / triggered burst searches
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline for triggered gravitational-wave (GW) burst searches, and presents preliminary results from Monte Carlo simulations. Triggered searches differ fundamentally from all-sky, untriggered searches because astronomical observations supply rich prior information (sky location, distance, burst type) and because the small data volume permits computationally expensive algorithms. The authors argue that these two features yield higher sensitivity and motivate the use of new conditioning and detection-statistic algorithms. RIDGE performs a two-step data-conditioning stage (running-median PSD noise-floor estimation, FIR whitening, and MBLT line removal) followed by a coherent network analysis based on regularized maximum likelihood. The detection statistic is computed over the full sky-map, with two candidate statistics compared: a maximum-to-minimum ratio (Rmm) and a radial-distance statistic (Rrad). Monte Carlo simulations use a four-detector network (H1, L1, H2, V1) with design-sensitivity PSDs, injected sine-Gaussian signals at the GRB060813 location, and show that Rrad substantially outperforms Rmm. For hrss = 5×10⁻²² Hz⁻¹ᐟ², the detection probability is about 62% at a false-alarm probability of 10⁻². The authors conclude that RIDGE provides an independent check on other pipelines and a platform for testing new regulators, and they note future work integrating waveform estimation. The paper is notable for describing the pipeline and algorithms in detail while explicitly deferring code description, and for reporting only preliminary simulation results without formal significance calibration.

Triggered searches can use richer priors and more expensive algorithms.
RIDGE provides an independent check and platform for new regulators.

Executive Summary
This paper introduces RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline for triggered gravitational-wave (GW) burst searches, and presents preliminary results from Monte Carlo simulations. Triggered searches differ fundamentally from all-sky, untriggered searches because astronomical observations supply rich prior information (sky location, distance, burst type) and because the small data volume permits computationally expensive algorithms. The authors argue that these two features yield higher sensitivity and motivate the use of new conditioning and detection-statistic algorithms. RIDGE performs a two-step data-conditioning stage (running-median PSD noise-floor estimation, FIR whitening, and MBLT line removal) followed by a coherent network analysis based on regularized maximum likelihood. The detection statistic is computed over the full sky-map, with two candidate statistics compared: a maximum-to-minimum ratio (Rmm) and a radial-distance statistic (Rrad). Monte Carlo simulations use a four-detector network (H1, L1, H2, V1) with design-sensitivity PSDs, injected sine-Gaussian signals at the GRB060813 location, and show that Rrad substantially outperforms Rmm. For hrss = 5×10⁻²² Hz⁻¹ᐟ², the detection probability is about 62% at a false-alarm probability of 10⁻². The authors conclude that RIDGE provides an independent check on other pipelines and a platform for testing new regulators, and they note future work integrating waveform estimation. The paper is notable for describing the pipeline and algorithms in detail while explicitly deferring code description, and for reporting only preliminary simulation results without formal significance calibration.

Research Context
Triggered GW searches differ from all-sky searches in key ways. Triggered searches have rich prior information from astronomy. Prior information includes sky location and burst type. Burst type guides the expected signal morphology. Small data volume enables expensive algorithms. Prior work used priors only in limited cases. Only one prior search used X-ray oscillations as a prior. Pulsar searches use Bayesian methods as a model. Prior information is underused in triggered searches.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper describes a new triggered-search pipeline. RIDGE uses new algorithms for conditioning and search. The pipeline is named RIDGE and is in MATLAB. The hypothesis is that full-sky statistics improve detection. Rrad should outperform the naive Rmm statistic. Prior information should raise sensitivity. The pipeline should be sensitive on a LIGO-Virgo network. RIDGE should serve as an independent check. Future work will add waveform estimation.

Methodological Details
The pipeline is called RIDGE. The pipeline is written mostly in MATLAB. The authors defer detailed code description. Triggered searches have several standard components. Trigger information collection is nearly automated in LSC. GCN triggers are a key trigger source. Prior information needs mathematical incorporation. The SGR-1806–20 search used X-ray oscillations as a prior. Pulsar searches use Bayesian approaches as a model. Data conditioning mitigates instrumental artifacts. Conditioning uses a two-step process. The noise floor is estimated with a running median. The noise floor is approximated by the LIGO SRD curve. The running median rejects outliers like power-line noise. Whitening uses FIR filters with PSD-derived coefficients. Filter coefficients come from a training segment. Non-stationarity can create filter discrepancies. Line removal uses the MBLT method. MBLT estimates line amplitude and phase. Line carrier frequencies are found manually. MBLT uses the running median to reject transients. Detection uses regularized maximum likelihood. The response is a combination of two polarizations. The inversion is ill-posed and needs regularization. The regularization scheme is from reference [10]. The output is a sky-map S(theta, phi). The network is H1, L1, H2, V1. Noise is Gaussian, stationary, and about 3000 sec. Noise is generated from four white-noise realizations. Instrumental artifacts are added sinusoids. Artifact frequencies are 54, 60, 120, 180, 344, 349, 407 Hz. PSDs use a 2.0 Hz frequency resolution. Signals are sine-Gaussian at 235 Hz with Q=9. The h-cross waveform has a pi/2 phase offset. The source is at theta=-30 degrees, phi=167.0 degrees. The source location is the GRB060813 trigger. hrss values are 3, 5, and 7 times 10 to the -22. Sampling frequency is 16384 Hz. Conditioning trains on the first two seconds. Data is processed in 0.5 sec segments. Injected signals last about 40 msec. The 0.5 sec integration is a lower bound. The large integration time accommodates filter delays. The filters are all FIR filters. H1 and H2 responses are identical due to co-location.

Procedures And Architectures
Conditioning estimates the PSD noise floor. The running median rejects narrowband outliers. Whitening uses a filter with unit-magnitude transfer. Whitening produces data with unit variance. Line removal targets power-line and violin modes. Signals are unaffected by line removal. The detection statistic maximizes over waveforms. The statistic is computed over the full sky-map. Rmm is the max-to-min ratio of the sky-map. Rrad is a radial distance in scaled space. Rrad uses the ensemble-mean sky-map S0. Simulations use a four-detector network. PSDs use design sensitivity curves. Detector locations and orientations are kept real. Noise is generated via FIR filters. Signals are injected at regular intervals. The signal is a single source. The h-cross phase is pi/2 relative to h-plus. Detector responses are shown in Figure 5. Conditioning applies anti-aliasing and whitening. Sky-maps are generated in 0.5 sec segments. The ROC curve compares Rmm and Rrad. Rrad outperforms Rmm. The enhancement is shown by arrows in Figure 6. Detection probability is about 62% at 10 to the -2 false alarm. The false alarm rate is one event per 50 sec. The pipeline reconstructs waveforms at any sky location. Future work integrates waveform estimation.

Key Results
The Rrad statistic outperforms Rmm. Full-sky statistics are required for triggered searches. Rrad is shown to beat Rmm in Figure 6. The enhancement is indicated by arrows. Detection probability is about 62% for hrss=5e-22. This is at a false alarm probability of 10 to the -2. The false alarm rate is one event per 50 sec. The result is for hrss = 5 times 10 to the -22. The pipeline is described as quite sensitive. The detection rate is 2 times 10 to the -2 per sec. The network is a LIGO-Virgo configuration. The signal is hrss = 5 times 10 to the -22. The magnitude scale is in arbitrary units.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Triggered searches can use more prior information. Prior information raises sensitivity. Small data volume allows expensive algorithms. Full-sky statistics are required for triggered searches. Rrad incorporates full-sky information. Rrad beats the naive Rmm statistic. The result demonstrates the value of full-sky statistics. Better full-sky statistics may improve performance. The 62% detection is a lower bound. The large integration time limits sensitivity. The pipeline is an independent check. RIDGE tests new regulators. RIDGE reconstructs waveforms. Waveform reconstruction enables astrophysical inference. The result is preliminary. The pipeline differs from other pipelines. The hard constraint statistic is used elsewhere.
